archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (barely)
archetype.definition: A bad team whose 2-7 is still a couple of wins worse than its scoring margin, sunk mostly by turnovers and a passing game that cannot move the ball, while the run game and hidden yardage quietly hold up.

report.headline: A functional run game buried under turnovers and a broken passing attack
report.take:
This is a team split cleanly down the middle on offense. Daniel Jones has started all nine games, and the passing game ranks 31st in EPA at -0.189, while the ground game behind Jonathan Taylor ranks 6th in rush EPA and 7th in run success. That is a startling drop for an offense that ranked 7th in EPA and scored 27.4 points a game in 2025. The closer historical match is 2022, when the Colts won four games with the 31st-ranked offense and the league's worst turnover margin. The current version is tracking very close to that.

The record is driven by giveaways. The offense has 17 turnovers and the defense only 6 takeaways, for a -11 margin that ranks 31st per game. Add a 0.2 win rate in one-score games, with losses of 30-33 at Kansas City, 20-26 to Tennessee, 10-16 at Minnesota and 23-27 to Dallas, and you get a team the point differential says should have 3.8 wins, not two. That gap, -1.79 wins over expected, is the noise. The 29th-ranked net EPA is the signal: even with neutral luck, this is a below-average team.

The raw numbers overstate how bad the defense is. Points allowed rank 30th at 27.7 a game, but on a per-play basis the defense is merely mediocre: 21st in EPA allowed, 13th in success rate allowed and 5th on third downs. What hurts it is big plays (31st in explosive pass rate), no pass rush (27th in pressure rate) and an offense that keeps handing over possessions. The side of the ball that is genuinely broken is the passing offense. The 25 sacks allowed and a QB hit rate that ranks 28th show the protection is part of that. So does a receiver room missing Alec Pierce, who has played only two games.

The schedule offers a pocket of relief: Miami now, and later Philadelphia at 2-7 and Tennessee at 1-7. The other five remaining games are against Houston, the Giants, Cincinnati, Cleveland and Jacksonville, all better teams. Turnover luck usually drifts back toward normal, so a few more wins are likely. A real turnaround would need the passing game to become merely bad instead of 31st. With right tackle Jalen Travis out for weeks and three defensive starters sidelined, nothing in the dossier suggests that fix is coming soon.

strengths.title: Efficient, staying-ahead run game
strengths.body: Taylor's 161 carries anchor an offense that is 6th in rush EPA and 7th in run success. The line gives decent help, with 4.1 yards per carry ranked 12th and a middle-of-the-pack stuff rate. This holds up because it doesn't depend on game script: the Colts are only slightly run-leaning relative to expectation, and the efficiency has come while they were trailing most weeks. Travis's knee injury is the threat to it.

strengths.title: Wins the hidden-yardage margins
strengths.body: Special teams rank 6th in EPA per game, the team commits the third-fewest penalties, and it ranks 8th in time of possession. That combination keeps games closer than the offense deserves, which is why the Colts cover more than half their spreads despite the record. These are process traits that tend to persist.

strengths.title: Third-down defense gets off the field
strengths.body: Opponents convert only 32.4% of third downs, 5th-best, and the success rate allowed ranks 13th. On a down-by-down basis the defense is fine; its point totals are inflated by explosives and turnovers rather than sustained drives. That said, the injuries to Davis-Gaither, Haulcy and Walley put this strength at risk in the short term.

concerns.title: The passing game and turnovers
concerns.body: Pass EPA ranks 31st, and passing EPA was negative in seven of nine games, including -21.3 in the 7-42 loss at Jacksonville. The 17 turnovers turn a weak offense into a losing team, because they hand short fields to opponents. Some of the turnover rate should cool, but the inefficiency underneath is real: it has held across all nine starts by the same quarterback.

concerns.title: Defense allows explosives, forces nothing
concerns.body: The defense ranks 31st in explosive pass rate allowed and 31st in takeaways, and the pass rush ranks 27th in pressure rate. A unit that cannot pressure the quarterback or force mistakes has to be perfect on every snap, and missed tackles rank 24th. Takeaways should tick up somewhat with normal bounces, but the lack of pressure is structural.

concerns.title: Protection, now without Travis
concerns.body: The line allows a QB hit rate that ranks 28th and has already given up 25 sacks, including six against Tennessee. Travis has played 93% of snaps and is expected to miss two to four weeks with a knee injury. That weakens the weakest part of the operation at the worst time.

trend.note: A 2-2 start built on a gritty division win and a road win at Washington gave way to a losing run since early October, bottoming out in the 7-42 loss at Jacksonville. The 23-27 loss to Dallas, with two takeaways, was a modest recovery rather than a turn.

nextGame.headline: Worst defense by EPA visits: the passing game has no excuse
nextGame.body:
Miami arrives with the league's worst defense by EPA allowed, 31st against the pass at 0.255 a play and last in success rate allowed. It has little pass rush, with 12 sacks (31st), and gives up nearly half of opponents' third downs. If the Colts' passing game is going to post a positive day anywhere, it is here. Tight ends have feasted against Miami, which allows 0.76 EPA per target to opposing TE1s (worst in the league), and that points straight at Tyler Warren. On the other side, Miami's offense ranks 26th in EPA, is among the most run-heavy in the league relative to expectation, and leaks sacks at a 9.3% rate. The Book has the Colts as small home favorites at -2.5 with a 40.5 total, which reads as two bad offenses in a grinder.

Availability tilts against Indianapolis's defense. Linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither (92% of snaps), safety A.J. Haulcy and cornerback Justin Walley are all out, and linebacker Jaylon Carlies is questionable with a neck injury. That strips the back seven just as a run-first opponent arrives. On offense, Jalen Travis is expected to miss weeks, Mo Alie-Cox is questionable and Alec Pierce remains on IR. Miami's Malik Willis, who has taken every snap, is questionable with a groin injury after a 13-of-25, 128-yard outing. Running back Jaylen Wright and cornerback Darrell Baker Jr. are out, and Baker's absence thins a secondary that was already struggling.

waysToWin.title: Attack Miami's sieve of a secondary
waysToWin.body: Miami ranks 31st in pass EPA allowed and 30th against deep throws. This is the softest matchup Jones has seen all year. Feeding Warren, Allen and Downs early can produce the positive passing day this offense has not had since Kansas City.

waysToWin.title: Field position through special teams
waysToWin.body: In a game with a 40.5 total, hidden yards matter. The Colts' special teams rank 6th in EPA per game, while Miami's rank 28th and are in the negative. Winning the kicking game can supply the short field this offense rarely creates for itself.

waysToWin.title: Make Miami's offense play from behind
waysToWin.body: Miami's offense relies on the run and gives up sacks at the 30th-ranked rate. An early lead forces a limited, possibly hobbled Willis to drop back, where even this middling Colts rush can get home. The Colts have recorded three sacks in each of their last three games.

waysToLose.title: Giving the ball away again
waysToLose.body: Miami's defense rarely takes the ball away on its own (29th in takeaways), so any giveaway here would be self-inflicted. The Colts have had multiple turnovers in six of nine games. In a low-total game, two giveaways can erase every other edge they have.

waysToLose.title: Depleted defense can't stop the run
waysToLose.body: Miami wants to run, and the Colts rank last in rush EPA allowed and last against lead backs. With Davis-Gaither, Haulcy and Walley all out, a mediocre Miami ground game could control the clock and keep the Colts' offense off the field.

waysToLose.title: Another one-score game slips away
waysToLose.body: This line projects a close game, and the Colts have won only 20% of theirs. If it stays tight into the fourth quarter with a backup right tackle in pass protection, the late-game failures that have defined their season could easily repeat.

nextGame.watch: Whether Jones and Warren finally produce positive passing EPA against a defense that is worst in the league against tight ends. If they can't do it here, the passing game's problem is structural.

restOfSeason.body:
The turnover margin and the one-score record are the parts most likely to improve. A -11 turnover differential and a 0.2 win rate in close games rarely hold at those extremes, and the gap between two wins and the 3.8 the differential implies suggests some wins are owed. The run game, special teams and penalty discipline are sustainable and will keep most games competitive. The passing game is the ceiling. At 31st in EPA with a banged-up line and a thin receiver room, it gives no reason to expect a jump back toward last year's level.

The schedule splits into reachable games (Miami, Philadelphia, Tennessee, and perhaps Houston and Cleveland) and likely losses against Cincinnati's 2nd-ranked offense, the Giants, and Jacksonville's 3rd-ranked defense. Expect the Colts to win a few of the soft games, score around 20 a game, and allow a bit less once the injured defenders return and the turnover flood slows. The likely landing spot is the bottom eight of the league rather than a late push.
swingFactors: Return of Davis-Gaither, Haulcy and Walley
Travis back at tackle by late November

confidence.note: Nine games with a stable QB make the profile readable, but the defensive injuries muddy the near term.
